title: Essay titles for revision
description: Three more essay titles from this week’s lectures. Note them down for revision, and write any of them here for practice.
instructions:
Optional, for revision. These are more essay titles that go with this week’s lectures. It’s worth noting them down, as they’re good practice for the exam. Only the Supervision 3 essay needs to be handed in.

  • You can write any of them here for practice, as you would in the exam: about 40 minutes each, without notes. You don’t need to answer all of them.
  • Planning an answer to each one (your argument, your evidence and the order you’d put them in) is good revision too.
  • After you submit, Review my answers shows you the ground each title covers.

questions.title: The force of a skeletal muscle
questions.text: What factors affect the contractile force developed by a skeletal muscle?
questions.guidance:
Here are some points to consider. It isn’t a model answer.

  • Size and architecture. Fibres and myofibrils lie side by side, so their forces add, and the maximum force of a muscle is proportional to the number of thick filaments in its cross-section, and so to its physiological cross-sectional area. Pennate muscles pack in more fibres than parallel-fibred muscles of the same volume, so they’re stronger, at the cost of range and speed. Training and disuse change force mainly by changing the cross-sectional area, though much of the early gain from strength training comes from the nervous system, which learns to recruit and fire motor units better.
  • Recruitment. The nervous system grades force by the number of motor units it activates. It recruits small, slow, fatigue-resistant units first, and large, fast ones only for greater forces (the size principle).
  • The frequency of stimulation. A twitch lasts much longer than the action potential that triggers it, so impulses that arrive before the muscle has relaxed summate. At high enough frequencies they fuse into a tetanus, several times as strong as a twitch, because Ca2+ stays high and the elastic elements in series with the contractile machinery are fully stretched.
  • Length. The length–tension relationship follows the overlap of the thick and thin filaments (Gordon, Huxley and Julian, 1966). Active force is greatest over a narrow range of sarcomere lengths, near the muscle’s working length in the body, and it falls when the sarcomeres are stretched (less overlap) or shortened too far (the filaments collide). Passive tension adds to the total at long lengths.
  • Velocity. Force falls as the velocity of shortening rises (Hill’s force–velocity relationship), because fewer cross-bridges are attached at once. It’s greatest in eccentric contractions, when the active muscle is being stretched.
  • Fibre type, fatigue and metabolism. Fast and slow fibres differ in speed and fatigue more than in force for their size. With repeated stimulation, force falls (fatigue), through reduced excitability of the membrane and impaired release of Ca2+ more than through running out of ATP. Temperature matters too.
  • Disease and drugs. Anything that breaks the chain from nerve to cross-bridge lowers force: myasthenia gravis (fewer acetylcholine receptors), curare, and the muscular dystrophies (fewer working fibres).
  • Evaluate. Distinguish the force of the muscle from the force it exerts at the hand, which the levers of the skeleton change. Which factors does the nervous system control from moment to moment (recruitment, frequency), and which are fixed by the muscle’s structure, or change only slowly (size, architecture, fibre type)?

questions.title: The sarcomere, and defects in its proteins
questions.text: Explain how the molecular organisation of the sarcomere enables skeletal muscle contraction and discuss consequences of defects in structural muscle proteins.
questions.guidance:
Here are some points to consider. It isn’t a model answer.

  • The structure. The sarcomere runs from one Z disc to the next. Thin filaments of actin, with tropomyosin, troponin and nebulin along them, are anchored by their plus ends at the Z discs, where α-actinin cross-links them. Bipolar thick filaments of myosin II, about 300 molecules each, lie in the middle, held there by titin, which runs from the Z disc to the M line. Explain the bands (A, I, H, M and Z) in terms of the filaments.
  • How the organisation produces contraction. Myosin walks towards the plus ends of actin, and the thick filaments are bipolar, so the two halves of each thick filament pull the thin filaments towards the middle, and the Z discs move together. The filaments slide: the A band stays the same length while the I band and the H zone narrow (the two papers of 1954). Explain the cross-bridge cycle and the part ATP plays in it. Rigor mortis shows that ATP is needed to detach the heads.
  • Regulation is built in. Troponin and tropomyosin on the thin filaments switch the cross-bridges on when Ca2+ rises, and the triads of T-tubule and sarcoplasmic reticulum lie beside the sarcomeres, so that Ca2+ has only a short way to go.
  • The organisation explains how muscle performs. The length–tension relationship follows the overlap of the filaments (Gordon, Huxley and Julian, 1966). Sarcomeres in series add their shortening and velocity, and myofibrils in parallel add their force.
  • Structural proteins. Titin is a molecular spring that gives passive tension and keeps the thick filaments centred. Nebulin helps to set the length of the thin filaments. α-Actinin cross-links them at the Z disc. Dystrophin links the actin cytoskeleton under the membrane, through a complex of membrane proteins, to the extracellular matrix, so that it passes force out of the fibre and protects the membrane.
  • Defects. In Duchenne muscular dystrophy there’s no dystrophin. The membrane is damaged by contraction, and fibres die and are eventually replaced by fat and fibrous tissue. Becker muscular dystrophy, with a shortened but partly working dystrophin, is milder. Mutations in titin cause some muscular dystrophies, and mutations that cut titin short are the commonest known genetic cause of dilated cardiomyopathy. Mutations in myosin, even ones that change its function only subtly, cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and mutations in nebulin are the commonest cause of nemaline myopathy.
  • Evaluate. Why do some defects show mainly in the heart, and others in skeletal muscle? Think about the different isoforms, and the fact that the heart never rests. What do the diseases tell us about what each protein normally does?

questions.title: Excitation–contraction coupling in skeletal and smooth muscle
questions.text: Compare and contrast mechanisms of excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal and smooth muscle.
questions.guidance:
Here are some points to consider. It isn’t a model answer.

  • What starts it. Skeletal muscle is excited only by its motor neurons, at the neuromuscular junction: acetylcholine acts on nicotinic receptors, and the end-plate potential triggers an all-or-none muscle action potential. Smooth muscle can be excited or inhibited by autonomic nerves (which release their transmitters from varicosities, with no discrete end plates), by hormones, local factors and stretch, and in the gut by slow waves from pacemaker cells, the interstitial cells of Cajal, which are coupled to the muscle. Its membrane may fire action potentials, or change its potential in a graded way, or not change at all.
  • Where the Ca2+ comes from. In skeletal muscle the action potential runs down the T-tubules, where dihydropyridine receptors act as voltage sensors, coupled mechanically to the ryanodine receptors (RyR1) of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The Ca2+ comes from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and extracellular Ca2+ isn’t needed. Smooth muscle has caveolae instead of T-tubules. Ca2+ enters through L-type channels when the membrane depolarises (electromechanical coupling), and transmitters and hormones acting on G-protein-coupled receptors make IP3, which releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum through IP3 receptors, with no change in membrane potential (pharmacomechanical coupling). Ca2+ that enters can also trigger more release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
  • How Ca2+ switches the myosin on. In skeletal muscle, Ca2+ binds troponin C, and tropomyosin moves to expose the myosin-binding sites on actin (thin-filament regulation), within milliseconds. Smooth muscle has no troponin. Ca2+ binds calmodulin, Ca2+–calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase, and phosphorylation of the regulatory light chain activates the myosin (thick-filament regulation). Caldesmon and calponin hold the thin filaments back until Ca2+–calmodulin relieves them, and the cell’s sensitivity to Ca2+ can itself be changed, by regulating the phosphatase that removes the phosphate.
  • Relaxation. In skeletal muscle, SERCA pumps return Ca2+ to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, where calsequestrin binds it, and the muscle relaxes quickly. In smooth muscle, Ca2+ is pumped into the sarcoplasmic reticulum and out of the cell, but the muscle relaxes only when myosin light-chain phosphatase removes the phosphate. Myosin dephosphorylated while it’s attached to actin forms latch bridges, which hold force while using little ATP.
  • Speed and grading. In skeletal muscle each action potential gives a twitch, switched on within a few milliseconds and at its peak within tens of milliseconds, and force is graded by recruitment and summation. Smooth muscle takes hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, and its force is graded by the level of Ca2+ and of phosphorylation. In unitary smooth muscle, excitation spreads from cell to cell through gap junctions.
  • Evaluate, with drugs and disease. Dihydropyridines such as nifedipine relax vascular smooth muscle, which depends on Ca2+ entry, but don’t stop skeletal muscle contracting. Dantrolene reduces the release of Ca2+ through RyR1 and is used in malignant hyperthermia. The two systems suit different jobs: fast, precise, voluntary movement on the one hand, and slow, sustained, economical control of hollow organs on the other.
